title: Sign-twisted FF world: monic denominators but numerator A with leading coefficient c ≠ 1

connection: DRINFELD_ES: degree-k Diff-parity over F_q(T) via rank-k Drinfeld modules. Carlitz torsion gives cyclotomic function fields where Frobenius of P is explicit.
why: In function fields, 'divisor of 4CP+1 in a class' is a Chebotarev statement in Carlitz cyclotomic extensions, with effective Chebotarev (Weil). This is the native tool.
first_step: State the function-field Type II at fixed level C as a Chebotarev condition in F_q(T)(Λ_{4C}) and compute the effective error.
area: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Power ladder ES_(k): cubic and higher rungs collapse to finite coverings
connection: POWER_LADDER_ES: for odd k, ES_(k) (x, y integers; the third term 1/z with z RATIONAL whose reduced denominator is Q^k, Q odd, gcd(Q,n) = 1; equivalently a third term Q^k/Z) is a finite congruence covering mod 4, while even k returns to ES^□. The native field is power-residue symbols and Waring-type coverings.
why: Calibration item: it shows exactly which relaxations are trivially true. A new rung (e.g. denominators in a norm group of a cyclic field) can be tested the same way.
first_step: Generalise: third denominator in N(K^×) for an abelian field K; find the index condition that makes the rung a finite covering.
area: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Matrix relaxation: 4/n = 1ᵀM⁻¹1 for integer positive definite M in a class (diagonal = ES)
connection: 1/x + 1/y + 1/z = 1ᵀ diag(x,y,z)⁻¹ 1. Replacing diagonal matrices by tridiagonal chain matrices gives 1ᵀM⁻¹1 = (tu + tv + uv + 2u + 2v)/(tuv − u − v). The problem 'every 4/n is 1ᵀM⁻¹1 for M in a class 𝒞' interpolates between ES and lattice problems.
why: For rich classes 𝒞 (all positive definite integer M) it is trivially solvable; for diagonal it is ES. The threshold class is a measure of how special the diagonal (Egyptian) structure is. 1ᵀM⁻¹1 is an effective conductance.
first_step: Test 𝒞 = {diagonal + one off-diagonal −1}: is every 4/p = 1ᵀM⁻¹1 for such M? Compute for p < 10⁴.
area: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Montesinos relaxation: Euler number −4/n with arbitrary numerators β_i (M(0; β₁/x, β₂/y, β₃/z))
connection: Allowing Seifert invariants (x,β₁),(y,β₂),(z,β₃) gives β₁/x + β₂/y + β₃/z = 4/n, which is trivially solvable. Requiring all β_i = 1 is ES; requiring β_i ∈ {1, 2} is an intermediate rung.
why: It gives a relaxation ladder native to Seifert/Montesinos knots, where the rung β_i ≤ 2 might be provable and might reveal which numerator constraint carries the difficulty.
first_step: Test 'β_i ∈ {1,2}' (i.e. 4/n = Σ ε_i/x_i with ε_i ∈ {1,2}) for all primes < 10⁷; find whether a uniform construction exists.
area: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Strengthen to induct: a stronger ES statement with an inductive parameter
connection: Thomassen proved 5-choosability by proving a much stronger precoloured statement that inducts. ES candidates: 'for every p and every prescribed residue r of x mod 8 (or of C mod 3), a certificate with that property exists' — check numerically which strengthenings hold, then look for an induction parameter (number of prime factors of 4Cp+1, size of e).
why: Often the right strengthening is what makes induction possible; numerics cheaply filter candidates.
first_step: Compute, for p ≤ 10⁶, which prescribed-property versions of (★)/ES hold for all p; keep the strongest surviving ones.
area: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Group-ring/Fourier formula for the window certificate count
connection: Olson's method works in group rings. For window e and N = Π q_i^{a_i} (coprime to e), the number of coprime divisor pairs (a, b) with ab | N and a ≡ −b (mod e) (the −1 branch; the full window condition also allows the target −p, PARITY_AUDIT §0 — reviewer repair) equals (1/φ(e)) Σ_{χ mod e} χ(−1) Π_i (1 + Σ_{1≤j≤a_i} (χ(q_i)^j + χ̄(q_i)^j)). A positive value gives an ES certificate at window e; the analogous formula with χ(−p) in place of χ(−1) handles the −p branch.
why: An exact character-sum formula for each window; non-vanishing is a statement about one finite character sum, open to zero-sum/Fourier techniques.
first_step: Implement the formula, verify against brute force, then study which characters dominate when the count is 0 for hard (p, e) pairs.
area: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Case-by-case → uniform: the small-n Bieberbach proofs were all different
connection: Before de Branges, each n (2–6) needed a different method; the uniform proof came from changing the statement (Milin's stronger conjecture). ES analogue: the repo's exponential families each needed bespoke windows; look for a stronger uniform statement (Milin-like) that implies all of them.
why: Suggests searching for the right stronger statement rather than more cases.
first_step: List the proved families (3·2^s+1, 7·4^s+9, 63·2^s+1, 4^s+k) and extract the common certificate mechanism; formulate a single conjecture implying all and test it on the open families.
area: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Ultraproduct transfer between F_q[T]-ES and ℤ-ES statements
connection: Ax–Kochen: first-order statements true for F_p((t)) for almost all p transfer to Q_p for almost all p. ES over F_q[T] has proved variants; ES is first-order over (ℤ, +, ·) (∀n ∃x,y,z), but Ax–Kochen transfers statements about valued fields (ℚ_p vs F_p((t))), not about ℤ with positivity; identify which ES-adjacent statements are about local/valued-field structures (and hence transferable) — reviewer repair.
why: Clarifies precisely which ES-type statements a model-theoretic transfer could ever reach (and that the full statement likely cannot).
first_step: Formulate ES sub-statements with bounded quantifier complexity (e.g. 'a certificate with C dividing a fixed polynomial in p') and check whether they are decidable/transferable.
area: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Precoloured version: ES with a prescribed denominator divisible by a given small prime
connection: Thomassen's induction works for a stronger precoloured statement. Candidate strengthening: for every prime p and every small prime r, there is an ES solution with r | x (or r ∤ any denominator). If such a refined statement holds numerically, its extra structure might allow an induction over r or over the e-slice.
why: Strengthenings with an inductive parameter are how many every-n combinatorial theorems were proved.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁶, check which (r, condition) refinements hold for all p; record the first failure for each.
area: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: q→∞ failure (Thm 2.1) ↔ few numerators per prime (Luca–Pappalardi, Mond–Portier A₃(p))
connection: ES_q(A,P) fails for a proportion → 1 of P as q → ∞ with deg P fixed; over Z, Σ_{p≤x} A₃(p) ≍ x(log x)³(up to loglog), so a typical p has only polylog numerators m with m/p a 3-term sum.
why: Both say 'numerator size vs denominator size' governs a phase transition; the Z regime m ≍ p^δ is the analogue of q→∞ and its failure would be the integer twin of Thm 2.1.
first_step: Read Mond–Portier 2201.11805 and check whether the proof shows A₃(p) is supported on m ≤ (log p)^C for most p — if so record the integer 'Thm 2.1'.

title: Unit fractions generate a DVR (Epstein): structure of R(D) for D = Z[1/S] and O_K
connection: Epstein shows the subring generated by reciprocals of a Euclidean domain is K or a rank-1 DVR. ES asks for specific 3-term representations; the ring R(D) records which 'unit fraction algebra' each world supports.
why: If R(D) ≠ K exactly in the hard worlds (e.g. F_q[T] where R(D) is the DVR at ∞), it gives an algebraic invariant correlating with ES-hardness.
first_step: Compute R(D) for Z, F_q[T], Z[i], Z[√2] from Epstein's theorem and compare with the hard/easy classification.

title: Egyptian integral domains (Guerrieri–Loper–Oman, Epstein): ES as a 3-term refinement
connection: An Egyptian domain is one where every element of the fraction field is a finite sum of distinct unit fractions. ES is the 'length 3 for numerator 4' refinement. The Egyptian-domain literature classifies which domains have the unrestricted property.
why: Their techniques (e.g. using units or integrality over Egyptian subrings) might yield length bounds, i.e. 'Egyptian length' functions whose Z-value at 4/n is ES.
first_step: Read 'From ancient Egyptian fractions to modern algebra' and Epstein 2303.15685; look for any length-bounded statement.
refs: Guerrieri–Loper–Oman, 'From ancient Egyptian fractions to modern algebra' (faculty.uccs.edu/goman PDF)

title: Egyptian length function ℓ_R(a/b) across domains R
connection: Define ℓ_R(q) = minimal number of unit fractions (with cone) summing to q. ES ⇔ ℓ_ℕ(4/n) ≤ 3. Compare ℓ over Z, F_q[T], O_K: maximal ℓ for numerator-k fractions.
why: A domain-independent invariant enables 'transfer' statements: e.g. ℓ_Z(4/n) ≤ ℓ_{Z[i]}-something.
first_step: Compute ℓ for numerator ≤ 8 fractions in Z and F_3[T] (monic) and compare distributions.

title: Best underapproximation of 4/n by three unit fractions (Kovač / Nathanson / Chu) — ES ⇔ gap 0
connection: The 'best k-term underapproximation' literature studies max{Σ_{i≤k} 1/x_i ≤ q}. ES ⇔ the 3-term underapproximation of 4/n is exact. Structure theorems for best underapproximations (eventually greedy) might constrain when exactness is possible.
why: If best 3-term underapproximations of 4/n are 'eventually greedy' in a way that forces a particular x, ES reduces to a single e-slice — testable.
first_step: Read Kovač 2406.07218 and Nathanson 2202.00191; compute the best 3-term underapproximation of 4/p for p ≤ 10^4 and check whether greedy first term works.

title: Shifted-prime denominators (Bloom): 4/n with denominators of the form q − 1, q prime
connection: Bloom proved results on unit fractions with shifted prime denominators (density/Ramsey type). The 3-term restriction 4/n = Σ 1/(q_i − 1) is a sparse constrained world.
why: A sparse world where heuristics predict finitely many solutions overall tests the lottery model calibration (expected count ≪ 1 gives failures).
first_step: Compute the expected number of solutions under the lottery model and compare with brute force for n ≤ 10^4.

title: Covering systems ↔ unit fractions (Z.-W. Sun): ES as a statement about AP packings
connection: Sun relates m-covers by residue classes to sums of unit fractions of moduli. Three pairwise disjoint APs with moduli x, y, z have density Σ 1/x_i; ES ⇔ some disjoint triple of APs has density exactly 4/n (disjointness needs at least pairwise gcd > 1, but this is neither automatic — (2,5,10) is an ES triple at n = 5 with gcd(2,5) = 1 — nor sufficient: periods (6,10,14) admit no three pairwise disjoint APs, since that would need three distinct parities).
why: Imports covering-system technology (Hough, Balister–Bollobás–Morris–Sahasrabudhe–Tiba distortion method) into ES via packings.
first_step: Determine for which ES triples disjoint residues exist (a CRT/graph-colouring condition on the gcds) and whether every p has at least one such triple; only then is 'ES ⇔ AP packing' an equivalence.

title: Elsholtz–Planitzer approximate parametrizations for k ≥ 4 unit fractions
connection: For sums of four and more unit fractions, Elsholtz–Planitzer use approximate parametrizations to count solutions. ES is the k = 3 case where exact parametrizations (Type I/II) exist.
why: Their counting lower bounds for k ≥ 4 may have a pointwise version at specific n; a 4-term pointwise result plus a merging step would be a new route.
first_step: Read arXiv:2012.05984 and 1805.02945; check whether any pointwise (fixed n) 4-term statement is proved.

title: Four-term ES with distinct denominators is trivial — but four-term with a size cap is not
connection: 4/n as a sum of 4 unit fractions is easy (e.g. via 3/n splitting). With all denominators ≤ C·n (no huge denominators), the 4-term problem becomes a lattice/lottery problem again.
why: Size-capped multi-term ES might be provable for k = 4 with C large while ES (k = 3) remains open, giving a tunable intermediate theorem.
first_step: Compute, for n ≤ 10^4, the least C such that 4/n has a 4-term representation with max denominator ≤ C n; test boundedness.

title: A₃(p)-numerator geometry: the set M(p) as lattice points under a hyperbola
connection: m ∈ M(p) iff m/p = Σ 1/x_i; for each Type II parameter set, the achievable m form arithmetic progressions. M(p) is then a union of APs intersected with [1, 3p].
why: If M(p) is a union of many APs with differences coprime to 4, it contains a multiple of 4 — a pigeonhole route to ES via the numerator direction.
first_step: For p ≤ 10^4 compute M(p) and fit it as a union of APs; inspect the differences mod 4.

title: Kraft–McMillan / compact trees ↔ sums of unit fractions (Elsholtz–Heuberger–Prodinger)
connection: Compact prefix codes and canonical trees are counted via sums of unit fractions; ES-type identities appear as specific tree shapes with three leaves of weights 1/x_i summing to 4/n.
why: A tree/code interpretation may give a bijective or generating-function handle on solution counts.
first_step: Read arXiv:1108.5964 to see which unit-fraction equations correspond to which trees; check whether 3-leaf subtrees encode ES.

title: Egyptian fractions in the Sierpiński triangle / Pascal mod 2
connection: Recent work connects Egyptian fractions to the Sierpiński triangle (De Carli et al.). A 2-adic/Lucas-theorem structure might organize 4/n representations by binary digits of n.
why: The 2-adic structure of ES (coordinate in 4Z ∪ (8Z − p), m = 8 coincidence) could match Pascal-mod-2 patterns.
first_step: Read arXiv:2412.09728 to see the precise correspondence and test whether ES solution counts correlate with binary digit patterns of p.

title: Conlon–Fox–He on an Erdős–Graham question about Egyptian fractions
connection: Recent work resolves an Erdős–Graham question on Egyptian fractions (details to read). It belongs to the modern 'Egyptian existence' toolkit along with Bloom and Liu–Sawhney.
why: Any new technique giving existence of Egyptian representations with structural constraints is a candidate input for constrained ES worlds.
first_step: Read arXiv:2404.16016 abstract and main theorem; note the technique.

title: Odd perfect numbers and abundancy: Σ_{d | n} 1/d = 2 as an Egyptian constraint
connection: σ(n)/n = Σ_{d|n} 1/d; perfect numbers solve an Egyptian equation with denominators forced to be all divisors. Bounds on odd perfect numbers (Nielsen) use unit-fraction inequalities.
why: Shares the 'Egyptian equation + multiplicative constraint' shape; techniques bounding solutions there bound ES-like constrained worlds.
first_step: Low priority: note as sibling.

title: Erdős–Selfridge/Graham 'Egyptian fractions with denominators in [N, cN]' as size-window sibling
connection: Problems asking for Σ 1/x_i = 1 with all x_i in a dyadic range relate to ES solutions whose denominators are confined to windows (p/4 < x ≤ 3p/4 etc.).
why: Window-confined existence results (Croot) are the closest analytic sibling to the ES window/slice structure.
first_step: Pointer: compare with Croot's short-interval result (batch C).

title: Sierpiński's 5/n, Schinzel's m/n: almost-all results (Vaughan) are uniform in m — what uniformity is known?
connection: Vaughan's density result covers every fixed m. The dependence of the exceptional-set bound on m is the quantitative sibling link between ES and its numerator neighbours.
why: A bound uniform in m up to (log n)^A would show the numerator-ladder (4 | 8 | 16) exceptional sets shrink together.
first_step: Read Vaughan 1970 for m-dependence; record.

title: Representation of 1 by k unit fractions: Sylvester/Curtiss bound and maximal denominators
connection: The largest denominator in Σ_{i≤k} 1/x_i = 1 is bounded doubly exponentially (Curtiss/Kellogg; Ambro–Barcau sharp bound for rationals). For ES the largest denominator is ≤ poly(n).
why: Sharp bounds on denominators (Ambro–Barcau) feed the size invariants (c(p) = max-denominator/p²).
first_step: Read arXiv:1412.3263 for their sharp bound specialized to 4/n with 3 terms.

title: Counting Egyptian fractions (Bettin–Grenié–Molteni): number of k-term representations of 1
connection: Precise asymptotics/lower bounds for the number of k-term Egyptian representations exist; ES counts (Elsholtz–Tao) are the numerator-4 three-term analogue.
why: Their methods (lattice point counting with Dirichlet series) may give secondary terms for ES average counts, sharpening the lottery mean.
first_step: Read arXiv:1906.11986 / 2509.10030 for methods; compare with Elsholtz–Tao's average counts.

title: Ternary Egyptian fractions with prime denominator: A₃(p) upper bound x(log x)³(log log x)² (Mond–Portier)
connection: Mond–Portier sharpen Luca–Pappalardi's upper bound on Σ A₃(p). Their method counts numerators per prime via the Type I/II parametrization and divisor sums.
why: Their divisor-sum machinery is directly applicable to the ES-at-p count; a pointwise lower bound for A₃(p) restricted to numerators ≡ 0 mod 4 is the needed statement.
first_step: Read 2201.11805 and check whether their method yields a lower bound for the number of m ≡ 0 (mod 4) in M(p) on average over p.

title: Partial-fraction world: 4/(T(T+1)(T+2)…) in Q(T) — Egyptian decompositions of rational functions
connection: Partial fractions decompose rational functions into sums of simple fractions A/(T − a). An 'Egyptian' decomposition requires numerators 1 and denominators in a semiring (e.g. monic polynomials with positive roots). This is a characteristic-0 FF-like world with residues.
why: Residue calculus gives exact conditions: Σ residues = coefficient conditions; may reveal a residue obstruction analogous to Lemma 1.1.
first_step: Determine when 4/(T − a) = Σ 1/X_i(T) with X_i monic in R[T] having real positive roots; compute residue constraints.

title: Coding-theoretic world: ES as a weight-enumerator identity for three cyclic codes of lengths x, y, z
connection: A cyclic code of length x has 'density' 1/x for a single codeword position class; a disjoint union of three such position classes with total density 4/n is the AP packing reformulation in coding language.
why: Mostly a rephrasing of the AP packing world; little added value.
first_step: Low priority.

title: k = 4 positive terms with all denominators ≡ 0 mod 4? ⇔ 16/n as a 4-term sum
connection: Generalizing all-even ⇔ 8/p: 4-term representations with all denominators divisible by 4 ⇔ 16/n is a 4-term sum. Divisor-closure across k-term worlds: (4d)/n with k terms ⇒ 4/n with k terms.
why: A k-term numerator ladder with k = 4 might be provable (more freedom), providing 4-term ES for all n — and a 4 → 3 merging step would be needed.
first_step: Compute exceptions of 16/n as a 4-term sum for n ≤ 10^4.

title: Merging step: from a 4-term solution to a 3-term one (when do two unit fractions sum to a unit fraction?)
connection: 1/a + 1/b = 1/c iff (a − c)(b − c) = c². Given many 4-term solutions of 4/n, ES follows if some pair satisfies this. The density of 'mergeable pairs' among 4-term solutions is a computable statistic.
why: Reduces ES to a statement about 4-term solutions (easier to construct) plus a quadratic coincidence; a 4-term family with a built-in mergeable pair would be a Type I/II family in disguise.
first_step: For n ≤ 2000 enumerate 4-term solutions with bounded denominators and count mergeable pairs; check whether every n has one (it must, since ES holds there).

title: k-term ES with prime denominators except one: Goldbach-flavoured world
connection: 4/n = 1/x + Σ_{i} 1/q_i with q_i primes: sums of reciprocals of distinct primes rarely have small denominators (the denominator is the product). So the world is nearly empty — a rigidity lemma.
why: Rigidity lemmas for prime-reciprocal sums (denominator = product of primes) explain why constrained worlds with prime denominators fail; useful for calibration.
first_step: Prove: Σ 1/q_i over distinct primes q_i (not dividing n) cannot equal 4/n − 1/x unless the q_i divide x·n — then enumerate.

title: Octonions / Cayley integers: non-associative ES — category check
connection: Unit fractions in a non-associative algebra are still defined (x⁻¹ = x̄/N(x)), and sums make sense, integer scalars still associate, so n·x scaling arguments survive; what may fail are arguments multiplying non-real denominators together (products of three octonions). The world is meaningful but its structure theory is thin.
why: Low value except as a test of which ES arguments use associativity (probably none beyond commutative subalgebras).
first_step: Low priority; note.

title: k-term FF: ES_q with 4 monic terms — does an FF finite covering exist for all q?
connection: With four terms the FF problem has more freedom; if four-term ES_q(A, P) is a theorem for all q via finite coverings, the FF world shows the '3 vs 4 terms' boundary exactly.
why: Locates the k-threshold for coverings in FF; over Z, 4-term ES with size constraints is the analogue.
first_step: Adapt the FF covering-tree search to 4 terms for q = 3, A = T, deg P ≤ 8.

title: Feature: monotone structure in the number of terms k
connection: Dividing-line feature 'monotone structure in the number of terms k'. ES ES is k = 3; k = 2 completely classified (Stewart); k ≥ 4 has power counts. To supply it one could: use the k = 2 classification as a sieve: ES(p) holds if some explicit p-tied integer N has a coprime-divisor pair (a,b) with 4 | a+b … i.e. reduce to many k = 2 problems
why: Interpolating between a classified and an open case is a classic route.
first_step: Formalise: ES(p) ⟺ ∃x: 4/p − 1/x is a 2-term fraction; apply Stewart's criterion to (4x − p)/(px) for x in [p/4, 3p/4].

title: Between: Ternary Egyptian for numerators m with all denominators in an AP
connection: 4/n = 1/x + 1/y + 1/z with x,y,z ≡ r mod q: local obstructions appear; which (q,r) still look universal?
why: Maps local obstructions vs global failures in a controlled family.
first_step: Compute for q ≤ 12 the residues r for which all n ≤ 10^6 coprime to stuff are solvable.

title: Minimal pair: k = 2 Egyptian (classified by Stewart) vs k = 3 Egyptian (ES, open)
connection: k = 2 Egyptian (classified by Stewart) vs k = 3 Egyptian (ES, open): they differ essentially in one feature — one more unit fraction: from a single divisor-class condition to a union over a 2-parameter family. ES's position: The k = 2 criterion is the gate; ES is a union of k = 2 gates.
why: Minimal pairs isolate the feature responsible for crossing the dividing line; each is a precise question about ES.
first_step: See 'k=2 reduction' feature item.

title: Erdős–Graham problem on 4/n with distinct denominators all ≤ n^{1+ε}?
connection: Bounding the largest denominator changes count; there might be literature on 'Egyptian fractions with small denominators' (Erdős–Graham book) for 4/n specifically.
why: A family where the count is tunable by the size bound.
first_step: Check Erdős–Graham 'Old and new problems' section on unit fractions for size-bounded ES variants.

title: OEIS anchors for 5/n and 6/n: A226644, A226645
why: The m-family is the Sierpiński/Schinzel generalisation; missing entries for m ≥ 7 are a gap a curator could fill and a sign the m-family data is unexplored.
first_step: Submit U_m(n) for m = 7..13 to OEIS (data in data/z52b/raw/m*_4000.txt) after checking against a second implementation.

title: 7/n fails only at n = 2 (≤ 10⁵ primes, n ≤ 4000)
connection: Consistent with PW (no 7/n exception in [3, 10¹³]); 7/p counts at primes are small (U₇(p) = 0,1,2,3,2,8,4,…).
why: 7/n is the smallest numerator where the local (mod-m) obstruction picture differs from 4 and 5; any ES method that is numerator-uniform must also handle 7.
first_step: Fit U₇(p) vs log²p and check whether the hardest 7/p primes coincide with the hardest 4/p primes.
refs: arXiv:2511.16817 (Pomerance–Weingartner, Exceptions to the Erdős–Straus–Schinzel conjecture)

title: Failure sets are monotone under divisibility of the numerator (sanity + structure)
connection: If m | m′ then fail(m) ⊆ fail(m′) (multiply all denominators of an m′/n representation by m′/m to get one of m/n); verified on all m ≤ 48, p ≤ 10⁵. 'Primitive' failures (not explained by a divisor d ≥ 5 of m) number 0,0,1,6,4,8,3,22,10,8,25,32,17,45,…
why: ES is the bottom of a divisibility lattice of Schinzel problems; primitive failure counts strip out inherited obstructions and are the right 'new difficulty' per numerator.
first_step: Submit primitive-failure counts to OEIS; examine whether primitive failures of 4k concentrate on primes hard for 4/p.
refs: arXiv:2511.16817 (Pomerance–Weingartner, Exceptions to the Erdős–Straus–Schinzel conjecture)

title: Hardness index H(p) = #{m ≤ 48 : m/p fails} correlates with U(p)/log²p (ρ = −0.43)
why: A single prime-level 'obstruction profile' across numerators: if hardness were a local (Euler-product) phenomenon, H(p) should be predictable from p mod small numbers — a cheap test of locality.
first_step: Regress H(p) on Legendre symbols (q/p) for q ≤ 30 and on p mod 8,9,16,25; report R².

title: Prime numerators have far fewer failures than composite ones
why: Composite m inherit failures from divisors (monotonicity) but also have fewer 'cheap' identities; the prime-m sequence measures the bare Schinzel difficulty.
first_step: Fit #failures(m) for prime m vs m (power law?) and compare with PW's exp(m^{1/3}) lower bound for n_m.
refs: arXiv:2511.16817 (Pomerance–Weingartner, Exceptions to the Erdős–Straus–Schinzel conjecture)

title: 10/n fails at {2,3,7,11,43,61,67,181}; 11/n at {2,3,4,37}; 13/n at {2,3,4,5,7,14,53,61,67,79,211,281}
connection: Complete-looking small exception lists (n ≤ 4000 all, primes ≤ 10⁵), none in OEIS; composite exceptions occur (4 for 11 and 13, 14 for 13).
why: Each list is a finite certificate target; the presence of composite exceptions (4, 14) shows the reduction-to-primes fails for m ≠ 4, unlike ES.
first_step: Explain 13/14 and 11/4 failures (why multiplicativity breaks) and check whether any composite n > 100 fails m/n for m ≤ 13.

title: 15/p failure set contains three of the 30 hardest ES primes (4201, 12601, 20521)
connection: 15/p fails at 25 primes ≤ 10⁵ ending 1103,1171,1367,4201,6301,12601,16831,20521; 4201, 12601, 20521 are top-30 hard for 4/p though 15 is not a multiple of 4.
why: Cross-numerator coincidence not explained by divisibility monotonicity; suggests a shared local cause (p ≡ 1 mod 120 or 840?).
first_step: Compute p mod 840 for 15/p failures and test enrichment of p ≡ 1 (mod 120).

title: Last-failure sequence by numerator m (7..48) is not in OEIS
why: These are lower bounds for Schinzel's n_m (true values may be larger beyond 10⁵); a curated table would let PW-type theory be compared with data.
first_step: Extend each m to 10⁷ (cost drops ∝ 1/m) and submit as 'largest known prime p with m/p not a sum of 3 unit fractions'.
refs: arXiv:2511.16817 (Pomerance–Weingartner, Exceptions to the Erdős–Straus–Schinzel conjecture)

title: Number of m/p failures ≤ 10⁵ by m: 0,0,1,6,4,8,3,22,10,9,25,38,17,49,16,63,… (no OEIS match)
connection: The failure-count profile across m (5..48) has strong arithmetic modulation (peaks at m ≡ 0 mod 12).
why: A Fourier/arith analysis of this profile would expose which local factors (mod 3, mod 4) drive Schinzel failures.
first_step: Regress log(#fail(m)+1) on log m and the indicator functions 4|m, 3|m, 5|m.

title: Composite-n failures for m ≤ 13 are only 4, 14, 25

title: Lattice attack on 'ES with x fixed to the greedy choice': when does greedy-first-term lead to a two-term remainder?
connection: The Fibonacci–Sylvester greedy picks x = ⌈n/4⌉; the remainder (4x−n)/(nx) with 4x − n ∈ {1,2,3} is a two-term sum iff a divisor condition on nx holds. For 4x − n = 1: 1/(nx) is one unit fraction, so greedy gives 2 terms? No: n ≡ 3 mod 4 case gives 1/(nx) — that's the easy class. For n ≡ 1 mod 4, 4x − n = 3 and 3/(nx) must split into two unit fractions.
why: The hard class p ≡ 1 mod 4 is exactly 'is 3/(p·⌈p/4⌉) a sum of two unit fractions, or else choose a non-greedy x'; the two-term criterion for 3/m is classical (3/m = 1/a + 1/b iff m has a divisor pattern mod 3). Making the 'non-greedy x' choice explicit is the whole game and the lattice view (x free, divisor of p²x² in class) is clean.
first_step: Tabulate for p ≤ 10⁶ the smallest x ≥ ⌈p/4⌉ such that (4x−p)/(px) is a two-term Egyptian fraction; study x − ⌈p/4⌉ distribution (is it O(log p)? polylog?).

title: Counting distinct unit-fraction solutions, not just proving existence

title: Group class equations naturally generate reciprocal sums
connection: MO 229514 notes that a finite group with n conjugacy classes gives a reciprocal sum equal to 1 using centralizer orders. This shares F01/F12/F14/F33: a structured family of unit-fraction representations arises from a symmetry object and its orbit stabilizers.

title: Frobenius finite exceptions and parameter stratification

title: Unit-fraction graph on ℚ: 3-step walks from 0 to 4/n
connection: Define the graph on ℚ_{>0} with r ~ r + 1/k. ES(n) ⇔ dist(0, 4/n) ≤ 3. Farey neighbours a/b, c/d satisfy c/d − a/b = 1/(bd), so unit steps between Farey neighbours are edges.

first_step: Compute the distance-2 neighbourhood of 4/p (pairs 1/y + 1/z) and its overlap with {4/p − 1/x}; record which Farey structure produces most certificates.

title: Fair-division reading (Rhind papyrus): 4 loaves among n people, each share as 3 unit fractions (not necessarily distinct)
connection: ES(n) ⇔ 4 loaves can be split among n people so that each share is exactly three unit-fraction pieces. This is the historical Egyptian 2/n-table problem generalised.

first_step: Compare the Rhind 2/n table's rules with Type I/II certificate selection rules (historical algorithms as certificate selectors).

title: Tetrahedral analogue: 1/r = Σ 1/h_i over four faces (four-term Egyptian in 3D)
connection: For a tetrahedron, 1/r = Σ_{i=1}^4 1/h_i (inradius vs altitudes). The triangle identity 1/r = Σ 1/h_i (three terms) is the 2D version behind the altitude form of ES. Higher-dimensional simplices give k-term Egyptian equations with geometric realisability conditions.
why: It places ES in a dimension ladder of simplex geometry, where realisability (simplex inequalities) adds constraints. Low priority, but it is a natural family.

title: Values of rational symmetric functions on ℕ³: e₂/e₃ = 4/n
connection: ES(n) ⇔ the rational symmetric function e₂/e₃ = Σ 1/x_i takes the value 4/n on ℕ³. Value sets of symmetric rational functions on integer points connect to Vieta-type substitutions and to the 'totally split cubic' item.

first_step: Write ES in (e₁, e₂, e₃) with 4e₃ = n·e₂ and study integrality of the roots via the discriminant; compute which (e₁, e₂) give totally split cubics for small n.

title: Diophantine approximation spectrum of 4/p by three unit fractions
connection: Schnirelmann-type arguments start from approximate representations. Define δ(p) = min_{x,y,z} |4/p − 1/x − 1/y − 1/z| over x,y,z ≤ p^A (A large enough that all solutions are included); ES(p) ⟺ δ(p) = 0. Study the gap structure of the set of values near 4/p.
why: If near-solutions are abundant at scale p^{−k} and the set of 3-term sums has a 'no isolated gap' property near 4/p, existence might follow by a continuity/pigeonhole step.
first_step: Compute the k smallest nonzero |4/p − Σ| for p ≤ 10⁵ and look for universal patterns in the residual numerators.
refs: Ramare, Ann. Scuola Norm. Sup. Pisa 22 (1995) 645-706

title: Nibble + absorber: random greedy first denominator, absorber for the two-term remainder
connection: Designs exist for all large admissible n via an approximate (nibble) decomposition plus a prepared absorber fixing leftovers. ES: choose x so that m = 4x − p is small and smooth (nibble-like), then 'absorb' via the two-term condition (m/(px) = 1/y + 1/z iff px has divisors a, b with a + b ≡ 0 mod m).
why: Separates ES into a flexible step (many x) and a rigid step (two-term splitting); quantifies how often the absorber succeeds.
first_step: For hard primes, enumerate x near p/4 with m ≤ M and measure the success rate of the two-term step as a function of the smoothness and divisor count of x.

title: Σ over the first denominator of a two-term representation function (ternary-Goldbach shape)
connection: Ternary Goldbach averages a binary problem over one prime: Σ_p r₂(n − p). ES: R_ES(p) = Σ_x r₂^{EF}((4x − p)/(px)), where r₂^{EF}(m/N) = #{1/y + 1/z = m/N} is a divisor-pair count (a + b ≡ 0 mod m over divisor pairs of N). The average over x is the extra variable that made Goldbach-type problems pointwise.
why: Makes the 'three-variable' structure explicit with a sum over a long free variable x ∈ (p/4, 3p/4), whose length is power-size even if the main term is not.
first_step: Compute for hard p the distribution of r₂^{EF} over x and the correlation between consecutive x; check whether the x-sum behaves like a sum of independent rare events.

title: Basis of order 3 vs order 4: Egyptian 'order' of 4/p is ≤ 4 trivially
connection: Schnirelmann bounds the order of a basis. For unit fractions, 4/p is always a sum of 4 unit fractions (4/p = 1/(k+1) + 3/(p(k+1)), and 3/m splits into ≤ 3 terms); ES asks for order 3. Study the 'order-3 deficiency': which 4-term representations of 4/p are 'one merge away' from a 3-term one (two terms with 1/a + 1/b a unit fraction)?
why: Turns ES into a merging problem on abundant 4-term representations, a different combinatorial entry point.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁵ enumerate 4-term representations with bounded denominators and count mergeable pairs; compare with the number of 3-term solutions.
refs: Ramare, Ann. Scuola Norm. Sup. Pisa 22 (1995) 645-706

title: Union-closed structure of the family of ES-solvable sets of numerators
connection: Gilmer's method applies to union-closed families. For each n, the set A_n = {m : m/n is a 3-term Egyptian fraction} — is the family {A_n} (or its complements) closed under unions/intersections in a way that forces a frequent element (a numerator m that works for most n)? For m = 4 the conjecture is 'all n'.
why: Odd, but the numerator–denominator incidence structure (with 8/n failing at 131, 241) is a natural set system to analyse with these tools.
first_step: Compute A_n ∩ [1, 30] for n ≤ 10⁵ and test closure properties and element frequencies.
refs: arXiv:2211.09055 (Gilmer, A constant lower bound for the union-closed sets conjecture)

title: Distinct-denominator and ordering refinements as stronger every-n statements
connection: Breusch/Stewart required distinct denominators of a given parity. ES refinements: x < y < z distinct (automatic except special cases), x ≤ p/2, z ≤ p²/2, gcd conditions. Determine the strongest refinement that still holds for all p ≤ 10⁹; it defines the 'tightest' every-p target.
why: The tightest true statement carries the most structure for a proof and the most information for disproof searches.
first_step: Tabulate, for p ≤ 10⁹, the minimal max-denominator over solutions normalised by p², and other extremal statistics.
refs: Breusch, A special case of Egyptian fractions, Amer. Math. Monthly 61 (1954) 200-201

title: Average over p of Schinzel-type events for the polynomials 4Cp + 1 in C
connection: Skorobogatov–Sofos average over polynomial families. At fixed p, the family {4Cp + 1 : C} is a linear polynomial in C; averaging over p (with C free) gives Schinzel-on-average-type statements on factorisations of 4Cp + 1 that underlie the almost-all ES theorem. Make explicit which 'Schinzel on average' input the almost-all proof uses and whether a pointwise-in-p version is a known open problem.
why: Locates ES exactly within the Schinzel-on-average landscape (what is averaged, over what).
first_step: Rewrite Vaughan's almost-all proof as a statement about factorisations of 4Cp + 1 averaged over p; identify the pointwise analogue.
refs: arXiv:2005.02998 (Skorobogatov-Sofos, Schinzel Hypothesis on average and rational points)

title: Function-field Type II ↔ binary quadratic forms over F_q[T] (Artin's imaginary quadratic function fields)
connection: Type II ES data encode representations by binary forms; over F_q[T] with q odd, binary forms have class groups of imaginary quadratic function fields (Artin). Class numbers are given by L-function values (RH known).
why: An FF formula 'ES count at P = combination of class numbers' with RH would give exact asymptotics, whose Z twin is a Dirichlet-class-number formula for ES counts.
first_step: Express the FF Type II count at fixed P as a sum over discriminants of class numbers h(D) and test numerically for q = 3.

title: Eisenstein cone: Z[ω] with denominators in the 60° sector
connection: Z[ω] has 6 units; angular sectors are not closed under multiplication (arguments add), so a positive cone must be a semiring such as N-spans of a few units, or a sector cone with a weaker closure requirement. Each choice gives a different Eisenstein ES.
why: Choosing a closed cone in Z[ω] is itself a non-trivial design question that tests which positivity axioms matter.
first_step: Determine the multiplicatively closed cones in Z[ω] discrete at ∞ (e.g. N-span of {1, −ω²}?) and run the e-slice search in each.

title: ES over Z[√−d] orders (non-maximal) with Gaussian-style cones
connection: Non-maximal orders (e.g. Z[2i], Z[√−3]) are not integrally closed; unit fractions behave differently at the conductor. ES for rational n in Z[2i] with Re, Im ≥ 0 sits between Z and Z[i].
why: Conductor primes give extra local constraints, a toy model of 'local obstruction at 2' that ES has with numerator 4.
first_step: Compare solution counts for rational p ≤ 10^4 in Z[i] vs Z[2i] cones.

title: Imaginary quadratic fields with class number > 1: ES for principal vs non-principal primes
connection: Over O_K with h > 1, a rational prime p ≡ 1 mod 4 may split into non-principal primes; then 4/p has fewer 'divisor' options among principal elements. With a sector cone this is a new hard world.
why: Measures the role of class group in the divisor-in-class lottery; Z has h = 1.
first_step: Take K = Q(√−5), sector cone, test ES for rational p splitting into non-principal primes vs principal ones.

title: Positive ES over O_K for n ∈ O_K with Galois-conjugate denominators only
connection: Require the three denominators to form a Galois orbit (K cubic, x, σx, σ²x): 4/n = Tr(1/x). Then ES becomes 'n/4 is the reciprocal of a trace of a reciprocal' — a norm-form equation.
why: Gives a cubic norm-form reformulation for rational n: Tr_{K/Q}(1/x) = 4/n; such equations are amenable to Thue/Schmidt or to equidistribution of units.
first_step: For cyclic cubic K of small conductor, solve Tr(1/x) = 4/p for totally positive x ∈ O_K, p ≤ 10^4.

title: p-adic sign patterns: which quadratic-character patterns (χ(x), χ(y), χ(z)) occur among local solutions
connection: Z_p carries no order, but a sign can be a quadratic character. ES over Z_p with denominators in a quadratic-character cone is a local question solvable by Hensel; relevant only as local data.
why: Local data are inputs to Bright–Loughran's no-BM result and the singular series; the cone version records which sign patterns of x, y, z occur locally.
first_step: Compute, for ℓ ≤ 30, which (χ(x), χ(y), χ(z)) sign patterns occur for local solutions of 4/n with n ≡ 1 mod 4 — compare with global solutions' patterns.
